editorial.hook: A knight plays chess with Death on a beach, and the game is the whole Middle Ages.
editorial.synopsis: A knight returns from the Crusades to a Sweden emptied by plague and finds Death waiting for him on a stony beach. He proposes a game of chess, to buy time — not to live, exactly, but to find out whether God exists before he dies. Across the country he and his squire fall in with a troupe of travelling players, a blacksmith and his wife, a girl about to be burned as a witch, and a procession of flagellants. Bergman films it in a hard, bright black and white that looks like a woodcut, and the famous images — the chess game, the dance of death on the hill — are stranger and funnier in the film than they are in memory.
editorial.whyItMatters: The film that made Bergman the figure of art cinema for a generation and the eleventh Criterion release; its imagery has been quoted and parodied so thoroughly that it is easy to forget how direct it is — a man asking Death for an answer and being told there isn't one.

editorial.hook: Two musicians flee the mob in dresses, and nobody in the film is quite who they say.
editorial.synopsis: Chicago, 1929. Two jazz musicians witness a gangland massacre and escape the only way they can think of: in dresses and wigs, with an all-girl band on a train to Florida. One falls for the band's singer, a ukulele player who drinks and loves the wrong men; the other is pursued by an elderly millionaire who will not take no for an answer. Wilder shot it in black and white because the make-up looked grotesque in colour, and the film moves at a speed that never lets you check the logic. Marilyn Monroe is luminous and sad at once. The last line is the most famous closing line in American comedy and the film has earned it.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 31 on TSPDT's list and the comedy most often named the greatest ever made; under the farce is a film about identity as performance that was decades ahead of its time, and Wilder's sharpest demonstration that structure, not jokes, is what makes comedy last.

editorial.hook: A Munich cleaning woman in her sixties marries a Moroccan worker, and the city stares.
editorial.synopsis: A widowed cleaning woman walks into a bar to get out of the rain and is asked to dance by a Moroccan mechanic twenty years younger than her. They marry. Then the film watches what the world does about it: her children, her neighbours, her grocer, her co-workers, each in turn freezing her out in a doorway, across a table, at the top of a stair. Fassbinder frames them in long still shots through door frames and railings, as if the whole city were a cage, and he lets the silence run. The second half turns the question around — what happens when the world stops staring and the couple are left with each other.
editorial.whyItMatters: Fassbinder's remake of Douglas Sirk's All That Heaven Allows made in fifteen days, and the film that proved melodrama could be the sharpest political form; number 52 on both Sight & Sound lists in 2022 and the gateway to the most prolific body of work in New German Cinema.

editorial.hook: Nine and a half hours of testimony about the camps, with not one frame of archive footage.
editorial.synopsis: Lanzmann spent eleven years making a film about the extermination of Europe's Jews without using a single second of archival film. Instead: the places as they are now — a clearing in a forest, a railway line, a village — and the people who were there, talking. A barber who cut hair inside the gas chambers, filmed cutting hair. A train driver who drew his finger across his throat at the Treblinka platform. A former SS officer, recorded with a hidden camera. Polish villagers who still live beside the sites. The film is nine and a half hours and it does not ask you to feel anything. It asks you to listen to how the thing was done, by whom, and how the land kept its silence.
editorial.whyItMatters: Twenty-seventh in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the film that redefined what a documentary could be: no footage, no narration, no reconstruction, only the present tense of memory — a method so absolute that nearly every film about atrocity since has had to answer to it.

editorial.hook: Twelve chapters of a Paris shop girl's fall, and a face in a cinema in tears.
editorial.synopsis: A young woman in Paris leaves her husband to try to act, fails, works in a record shop, runs out of rent money, and slides into prostitution — told in twelve numbered tableaux with intertitles, like a novel or a case study. Godard films Anna Karina, his wife, from behind in the first scene so that you spend the film waiting for her face, and when it comes it does the film's work: in a cinema watching Dreyer's Joan of Arc with tears running down it; dancing alone around a pool table; listening to a philosopher explain language in a café. It is cold in method and devastated underneath. Michel Legrand's theme keeps starting and stopping as if it cannot bear to finish.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1962 and the Grand Jury Prize at Venice; the most emotionally direct film of Godard's first period and the one where his method — Brecht's distance, documentary's surfaces, a woman's face as the subject of cinema itself — came together without irony.

editorial.hook: Postwar Vienna in tilted shadows, a zither, and a friend who turns out not to be dead.
editorial.synopsis: A broke American writer of pulp Westerns arrives in occupied Vienna to take a job from his old school friend, and arrives in time for the funeral. The friend was hit by a car; the witnesses don't agree on how many men carried the body. The writer starts asking questions, falls for the dead man's girlfriend, and is told by everyone — a British major, a Romanian, a baron — to go home. Carol Reed shot the city at night, in rubble and wet cobbles and Dutch angles, and scored the whole thing to a single zither, which should not work and does. The sewer chase, the Ferris wheel speech about cuckoo clocks and the final shot down an avenue of bare trees are each, on their own, reasons the film is still watched.
editorial.whyItMatters: Grand Prix at Cannes in 1949 and the film that gave the postwar world its visual shorthand for moral collapse; written by Graham Greene, with an Orson Welles performance that is on screen for perhaps ten minutes and defines the film.

editorial.hook: A man drives around the hills above Tehran looking for someone to bury him in the morning.
editorial.synopsis: A middle-aged man drives a Range Rover slowly through the dusty hills on the edge of Tehran, stopping to offer men a lift and then a job: he has dug a hole and intends to lie in it that night, having taken pills, and he needs someone to come at dawn and either help him out or cover him with earth. A young soldier runs away. A seminarian argues. An old taxidermist tells him about the taste of mulberries. Kiarostami shoots almost the entire film inside the car, in long two-shots, often filming the actors separately so that each was talking to him, not to each other. Why the man wants to die is never said. What the film is about is whether anything can be said to him.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1997 and the film that made Kiarostami the most argued-about director of the decade; its ending — which breaks the frame of the fiction entirely — divided critics for years and now looks like one of the bravest decisions in modern cinema.

editorial.hook: An English couple drive through Naples to sell a villa; the marriage comes apart.
editorial.synopsis: A wealthy English couple arrive in Naples to sell a dead uncle's villa and discover, alone together in a foreign place for the first time in eight years, that they have nothing to say to each other. She visits museums and catacombs and the sulphur fields and is shaken by them; he flirts in Capri and is bored. Rossellini gives them almost no plot, just the city — statues, bones, a pregnant woman in the street, the casts of a couple embracing at Pompeii — pressing on two people who have been avoiding themselves. Ingrid Bergman, who had left Hollywood for Rossellini, plays a woman watching her life from outside. The ending, in a crowd at a religious procession, is a miracle or a convenience, and the film refuses to say which.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1955 and the film the French New Wave claimed as its origin — Rivette wrote that with it 'all films have suddenly aged ten years'; its loose, searching, plotless modernity is the bridge from Neorealism to Antonioni, and it has never stopped looking new.

editorial.hook: A day in a Soviet city, filmed by a camera that keeps turning around to film itself.
editorial.synopsis: A city wakes: shutters, a woman washing, machines starting, a tram. A cameraman with a tripod over his shoulder climbs a smokestack, lies on the tracks under a train, rides in a car filming another car. Vertov's film has no actors, no story and no intertitles, only a day in the life of a modern city — Moscow, Kyiv and Odesa spliced into one — and the man and woman making the film about it, shown shooting and cutting it. Split screens, freeze frames, superimpositions, a camera that walks on its own tripod legs. It was meant as a manifesto for a cinema freed from theatre and literature, and nearly a century later it is still faster and more inventive than almost anything made since.
editorial.whyItMatters: Ninth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll — the highest-placed documentary ever — and the founding text of the idea that the camera's own act of seeing can be a film's subject; its influence runs through every city symphony, essay film and self-aware montage.

editorial.hook: Two girls decide the world is spoiled, so they will be too. Then they eat everything.
editorial.synopsis: Two young women, both called Marie, sit by a pool like puppets and decide that since the world has gone bad, they will go bad as well. What follows is a series of pranks and feasts: they let old men take them to dinner and eat everything on the table, cut up sausages and bananas with scissors, bathe in milk, set a room on fire, swing from a chandelier, and finally destroy a banquet laid for the Party elite — then try, giggling, to put it back together. Chytilová changes the film stock and tint from shot to shot, cuts on whims, and refuses every rule of character or plot. It was banned for 'depicting the wanton'. It is seventy-four minutes long and feels like a dare.
editorial.whyItMatters: Twenty-eighth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the wildest film of the Czech New Wave; a feminist and anarchist collage that the authorities understood perfectly, and whose formal abandon has influenced everyone from Agnès Varda to music video.

title: Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans

editorial.hook: A farmer plans to drown his wife, loses his nerve, and falls back in love in a day.
editorial.synopsis: A woman from the city is holidaying in a lakeside village and has got a farmer under her spell: drown your wife, she tells him, sell the farm, come with me. He takes his wife out in the boat. He can't do it. And then — in the film's great reversal — the terrified wife runs from him onto a tram to the city, he follows, and over one day in the city, through a church, a photographer's studio, a barbershop and a fairground, they find each other again. Murnau, brought from Germany to Hollywood with a blank cheque, built an entire city on a studio lot and moved the camera as no American film had, through marshes and streets and a tram ride that is one of the most beautiful shots in silent cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Eighth on TSPDT's aggregated list and the peak of silent film's visual art — the first film to win an Academy Award for 'Unique and Artistic Production', a category never offered again; its camera movement and expressionist light changed how Hollywood looked.

editorial.hook: A bored husband runs off with the babysitter, in primary colours and gunfire.
editorial.synopsis: A man walks out of a Paris party where everyone talks in advertising slogans, drives the babysitter home, finds a corpse in her flat, and leaves for the south of France with her the next morning in a stolen car. There are gangsters after her, or after something. They torch the car, live in a shack by the sea, read aloud, sing, quarrel; he writes a diary, she wants to dance. Godard shoots it in reds, blues and yellows so flat and bright they look like comic panels, and lets Belmondo and Karina break into song or address the camera whenever they like. It is a love story, a road movie and a suicide note for a certain idea of romance, and it ends in a flash of blue sky.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1965 and the last and most ravishing of Godard's films with Anna Karina — the end of their marriage is in it; its collage of pop colour, quotation and sudden violence is the hinge between his romantic period and the political films that followed.

editorial.hook: Every word sung, every wall a different colour, and the story is ordinary heartbreak.
editorial.synopsis: A seventeen-year-old who works in her mother's umbrella shop in a grey Norman port is in love with a mechanic who is about to be called up for Algeria. Every line of dialogue — about petrol, about rent, about love — is sung, to Michel Legrand's score, and Demy painted the real town to match: wallpaper, raincoats and bicycles in pinks, acid greens and tangerines. The plot is as plain as a letter home: a departure, a wait, a pregnancy, a proposal from someone else. The music and colour don't sweeten it; they make the ordinariness unbearable. The last scene, at a petrol station in the snow, is the saddest happy ending in cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1964 and the film that proved a musical could be as serious about loss as any drama; Demy's conception — the sung-through everyday, the colour as emotion — is the direct source of La La Land and of every film that has tried to make heartbreak beautiful without lying about it.

editorial.hook: A woman in Pennsylvania coal country drifts out of her life and into a stranger's crime.
editorial.synopsis: A woman in a Pennsylvania mining town shows up late to her own divorce hearing, agrees to everything, and walks out of her life — into a bar, a man's car, a motel, another man's car. One of them is a petty criminal who treats her with contempt and lets her stay, and she drifts along with his plan for a bank robbery because it is something to do. Barbara Loden wrote it, directed it and plays Wanda, shooting on 16mm with a crew of four, and she refuses every chance to make her heroine brave or pitiable. The film just stays with her — in diners, in fields, with her hair in curlers — with a patience and lack of judgement that still feels radical.
editorial.whyItMatters: Loden's only film, ignored on release and now 48th in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll; the founding work of American independent cinema by a woman, and a portrait of passivity so honest that Marguerite Duras called it a miracle.

editorial.hook: Letters from a travelling cameraman about Tokyo, Guinea-Bissau and memory.
editorial.synopsis: A woman reads letters from a cameraman who travels the world, mostly between Tokyo and West Africa, and the images are what he filmed: a ferry full of sleeping Japanese, a ceremony for broken dolls, a market in Bissau, a cat shrine, people on a Cape Verde pier looking into the camera, Hitchcock's San Francisco locations revisited, a video synthesiser that turns footage into coloured smoke. The letters are about how we remember and why we forget, about happiness and the way history erases the people who lived it. Marker invented a form here — the essay film — and no one has used it better. It is dense enough to watch twenty times and you will not reach the bottom.
editorial.whyItMatters: Fifty-ninth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the definitive essay film; everything from Herzog's late documentaries to the video essay as a genre stands downstream of Marker's method — image, voice and thought held in a conversation none of them wins.

editorial.hook: A couple in winter Venice, grieving a drowned child, and a small figure in a red coat.
editorial.synopsis: An English couple lose their small daughter in a pond at home, and some months later are in Venice for the winter, where he is restoring a church. Two elderly sisters, one blind and psychic, tell the wife that the child is with them and happy. The husband scoffs and keeps seeing, down alleys and across canals, a small figure in a red coat. Roeg cuts the film like a mind under stress — a love scene intercut with the couple dressing afterwards, water and glass and red recurring until they seem to mean something — and Venice in off-season is damp stone and fog and churches closed for repair. It is a ghost story that is really about the mathematics of grief, and the last ten minutes are a trap the whole film has been laying.
editorial.whyItMatters: Forty-sixth in the 2022 directors' poll and the high point of Roeg's fractured, associative editing; a horror film built from a Daphne du Maurier story that has influenced everyone from Kubrick to Lynne Ramsay, and the model for the idea that the cut itself can be the ghost.

editorial.hook: The Tramp versus the assembly line, and a last walk down a road into the sunrise.
editorial.synopsis: A factory worker on an assembly line tightens bolts until his body keeps doing it after the belt stops, is fed by a machine, gets sucked through the gears, and is sent to an asylum. Out of it, he picks up a red flag that fell off a truck and finds himself leading a Communist march. Chaplin made it nine years after sound arrived and still refused to let the Tramp speak — except, finally, to sing a song in no language at all. The factory sequences are the great visual satire of industrial life; the scenes with the orphaned 'gamin', played by Paulette Goddard, are the warmest Chaplin ever filmed. The last shot, two people walking down a road toward the horizon, is the Tramp's goodbye.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 51 on TSPDT's list and the last silent film from the man who had defined the form; Chaplin's clearest political statement and the final appearance of the most famous character in cinema, built from a decade of refusing to join the sound era.

editorial.hook: New York in long static shots, while a mother's letters from Brussels are read.
editorial.synopsis: Static shots of New York in the mid-1970s: a subway car, a diner at night, a street in Hell's Kitchen seen from a slowly moving car, the Staten Island ferry pulling away from Manhattan. Over them, Akerman reads letters her mother wrote from Brussels while she was living there — about the weather, the shop, an aunt's illness, whether she is eating, when she is coming home — in a flat voice sometimes drowned out by traffic. That is the whole film. The gap between the images and the letters is where it lives: a city that doesn't know she exists, and a mother who thinks of nothing else. The final shot, the skyline receding into haze for ten minutes, is one of the great endings.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 52 on both Sight & Sound lists in 2022; a film that made distance itself its subject and showed how much a fixed camera and an off-screen voice can hold — the formal key to Akerman's cinema, and the ancestor of a whole school of diaristic, durational film.

editorial.hook: A ballerina asked to choose between dancing and love, in blazing Technicolor.
editorial.synopsis: A young dancer joins a ballet company run by an impresario who believes art demands everything, and a young composer joins it at the same time. The impresario builds a ballet around her — The Red Shoes, from the Andersen story about shoes that will not stop dancing — and the fifteen-minute ballet at the film's centre leaves the stage behind entirely, becoming a nightmare of newsprint storms and dancing shadows. Then the dancer falls in love with the composer, and the impresario cannot bear it. Powell and Pressburger shot it in Technicolor so rich it seems to glow from inside, and Moira Shearer, a real ballerina, plays a woman asked a question no one should be asked.
editorial.whyItMatters: Forty-fourth in the Criterion Collection's catalogue and the film Scorsese has called the one he returns to most; the greatest film about art's cost, and the one whose colour and ballet sequence set the ceiling for what cinema could do with spectacle in service of feeling.

title: The Gospel According to St. Matthew

editorial.hook: The life of Christ by a Marxist atheist, in Italian villages with peasant faces.
editorial.synopsis: Pasolini filmed the Gospel of Matthew word for word — no added dialogue — in the hill towns of Basilicata, with non-actors: a Spanish economics student as Jesus, Pasolini's own mother as the older Mary, farmers and fishermen as the apostles. The camera is handheld and close, like a newsreel from the first century; the music runs from Bach to Odetta to a Congolese mass. His Christ is angry, impatient, a political preacher who walks fast and talks faster, and the Sermon on the Mount is delivered in a storm of jump cuts across changing skies. The Vatican newspaper called it the best film ever made about Jesus. Pasolini, a Communist and an unbeliever, dedicated it to Pope John XXIII.
editorial.whyItMatters: Grand Jury Prize at Venice 1964 and the film that made Pasolini's method clear — sacred subjects in the faces of the poor, shot with the directness of Neorealism and the rhythm of a poem; a model for the religious film without piety, from Scorsese to Reygadas.

editorial.hook: Two lovers in Dakar dream of Paris, on a motorcycle with a zebu skull on the handlebars.
editorial.synopsis: A young cowherd rides a motorcycle with a cow's skull mounted on the handlebars through Dakar, and a university student falls in with him; they want to get to Paris, where everything is, and they spend the film trying to raise the money — stealing clothes, stealing a cashbox that turns out to be full of a fetish, stealing a car from a rich man who wanted the boy for himself. Mambéty cuts it like a dream and a riot at once: the sound of waves over the city, Josephine Baker's 'Paris, Paris' on repeat, slaughterhouse footage against love scenes, the lovers imagined returning in triumph in an open car. It is funny, cruel, formally fearless and about as free as cinema has ever been.
editorial.whyItMatters: Sixty-sixth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the founding film of African modernist cinema; Mambéty made it for almost nothing and made only one other feature, and its influence — on everything from the Dardennes to Beyoncé's visual albums — far outruns how many people have seen it.

editorial.hook: A doctor's wife spends afternoons in a brothel; the film won't say what's real.
editorial.synopsis: A beautiful, cool young wife in Paris loves her surgeon husband and cannot bear to be touched by him. She daydreams of being whipped by coachmen. Then she hears of a discreet brothel that takes clients in the afternoons, and she begins working there from two to five, under the name Belle de Jour, going home in time for dinner. Buñuel films it in a flat, elegant, bourgeois style — Catherine Deneuve in Yves Saint Laurent, soft light, no music at all — and moves between her fantasies and her afternoons without marking which is which, until a gangster with metal teeth arrives and the two start to leak into each other. The last scene can be read three ways and the film declines to choose.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1967 and Buñuel's most popular film; a study of desire that refuses both judgement and explanation, and the performance that made Deneuve the face of a certain kind of European cinema — surface perfect, interior unreadable.

editorial.hook: Frankenstein comes to a Castilian village, and a girl goes looking for the monster.
editorial.synopsis: Castile, 1940, just after the Civil War. A travelling projectionist shows Frankenstein in the village hall, and a six-year-old girl is undone by it — not frightened, exactly, but shaken that the monster was killed. Her older sister tells her the monster is a spirit who lives in an abandoned sheepfold outside the village. She goes to look. Erice films the family's house in honey-coloured light through hexagonal windows like the cells of a hive, the father tending bees and writing at night, the mother writing letters to someone who may be dead; nobody speaks of the war and it is in every frame. Ana Torrent's face, watching, is one of the great faces in cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 85 in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the film that found a way to speak under Franco's censorship — a child's fairy tale as political mourning; its influence on del Toro's Pan's Labyrinth and on every film that has used a child's eyes to see history is direct.

editorial.hook: A simple girl is sold to a travelling strongman, and the road is their whole world.
editorial.synopsis: A poor mother on the Italian coast sells her slow, trusting daughter to a travelling strongman for ten thousand lire, as she sold her older sister before. He breaks chains with his chest in village squares; she learns to play a drum and a trumpet and announce him. He treats her like a dog and she stays, because where else is there. Then they fall in with a circus and a tightrope walker called the Fool, who tells her that even a pebble has a purpose. Fellini shot it in winter on real roads with Anthony Quinn as the brute and his wife Giulietta Masina as the girl — a clown's face with a saint's eyes — and Nino Rota's trumpet theme does the rest.
editorial.whyItMatters: The first winner of the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film and the film that took Fellini out of Neorealism into fable; Masina's Gelsomina is one of the handful of screen performances that people who have seen the film cannot describe without stopping.

editorial.hook: A love story between a soldier and a country boy, then a different film in the jungle.
editorial.synopsis: A soldier posted to a rural Thai town and a young man from the country fall slowly in love — motorcycle rides, a cinema, a cave temple, hands touching in the dark of a cab. Then, halfway through, the film stops, the title card appears again, and a second film begins: a soldier alone in the jungle, tracking a shaman who can turn into a tiger, with no dialogue, only the night sounds and a few intertitles. Apichatpong never explains how the halves connect, and the connection is the film's whole feeling — that desire is also a kind of hunting, that to love someone is to be lost in a forest with them. The tiger, when it comes, looks straight into the camera.
editorial.whyItMatters: Jury Prize at Cannes 2004 and Cahiers' film of the year; the film that announced Apichatpong as the most original director of the century so far, and the clearest statement of his method — two films that refuse to be reconciled, and are more true together than either alone.

editorial.hook: A Texas childhood in the 1950s, and in the middle of it, the birth of the universe.
editorial.synopsis: A family in Waco, Texas, in the 1950s: a father who loves his three sons and crushes them, a mother who is all grace and no power, and the eldest boy, caught between them, learning what cruelty is by trying it. A telegram arrives. And then Malick does the thing nobody had done — leaves the family for twenty minutes to show the formation of galaxies, the first cells, dinosaurs on a riverbank, before returning to a boy on a lawn. The camera never stops moving, whispered voice-over asks God questions, and the 1950s sequences are the most exact rendering of childhood memory in cinema — the way a sprinkler looked, the way a father's hand felt on your neck.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 2011 and the film that split audiences and critics down the middle; a spiritual autobiography on the scale of 2001, and the source of a whole visual language — gliding camera, magic-hour light, whispered prayer — that a decade of cinema and advertising has borrowed from.

editorial.hook: A man walks out of the desert after four years of silence, looking for his son.
editorial.synopsis: A man in a red cap and a ruined suit walks out of the Texas desert and collapses in a bar. His brother flies in from Los Angeles to collect him; he does not speak for days. He has been missing for four years. Slowly, on the drive back and in his brother's house, he returns to the world, and to the seven-year-old son who has been raised as someone else's. Then he and the boy set off to find the boy's mother. Wenders films America through a German's eyes — motels, freeways, neon, Ry Cooder's slide guitar over emptiness — and the long scene near the end, in a peep-show booth, in which two people speak through one-way glass, is one of the great scenes about what love did to them.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1984 and the film in which the New German Cinema's fascination with America became an American film; Harry Dean Stanton's only lead role and Sam Shepard's script gave Wenders his most complete work, and its images of the West have been copied ever since.

editorial.hook: A dead screenwriter narrates from a swimming pool; a silent star put him there.
editorial.synopsis: A struggling screenwriter dodging repo men pulls into the driveway of a decaying mansion on Sunset Boulevard and finds a silent-film star who has been forgotten for twenty years and does not know it, attended by a butler who was once her director — played by Erich von Stroheim, who once was. She has written a script for her comeback. He stays to fix it, then stays because he is kept. Wilder narrates it from beyond the grave with the sharpest voice-over in Hollywood, and Gloria Swanson, a real silent star in a real kind of exile, plays Norma Desmond with a courage that makes the monster unbearably human. 'I am big. It's the pictures that got small.'
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 41 on TSPDT's list and the film Hollywood made about its own cruelty; Louis B. Mayer reportedly screamed at Wilder for making it, and its image of a star drowning in her own myth has been the template for every film about fame since.

editorial.hook: A woman leaves her husband, her lover and her past, in long still takes.
editorial.synopsis: A former singer in Copenhagen tells her husband, a lawyer about to become a minister, that she is leaving him because he does not love her enough. She is in love with a young composer, who it turns out does not love her enough either. An old lover, a poet, returns to town to be honoured and would like her back; he did not love her enough then. Dreyer films all of this in takes of unprecedented length, the characters sitting side by side on sofas, barely looking at each other, speaking in a slow formal cadence that was booed at the Paris premiere. It is a film about a woman who asks for everything and will accept nothing less, told at the pace of her refusal.
editorial.whyItMatters: Dreyer's last film and Cahiers' second-best of 1964; dismissed as a senile failure on release and now 95th on TSPDT's list — the purest statement of the long-take, stripped-down cinema that Akerman, Straub-Huillet and the slow cinema directors built on.

title: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb

editorial.hook: A general launches a nuclear strike, and the War Room tries to stay polite.
editorial.synopsis: A US Air Force general, convinced that fluoridation is a Communist plot against his precious bodily fluids, orders his bombers to attack the Soviet Union and seals his base. In the Pentagon's War Room — a vast black set with a ring of light that Ken Adam designed and that Reagan reportedly asked to see on taking office — the President, a hawkish general and a wheelchair-bound ex-Nazi weapons scientist try to call the planes back while learning about a Soviet doomsday device. Peter Sellers plays three of them. Kubrick had set out to make a serious thriller and found the subject could only be approached as farce, and the result is the funniest film ever made about the end of the world.
editorial.whyItMatters: Forty-sixth in the 2022 directors' poll and the model for political satire ever since; made the same year as Fail Safe and the Cuban Missile Crisis's aftermath, it said what no serious film could — that the system was insane — and the ending, to 'We'll Meet Again', is still the bleakest joke in cinema.

editorial.hook: A Paris secretary with nowhere to go in August, and a flash of green at sunset.
editorial.synopsis: A secretary in Paris has her summer plans cancelled two weeks before the holidays and spends August trying to be somewhere — a friend's family in Cherbourg, where she is miserable; the mountains, which she leaves after a day; Biarritz, where she can't talk to anyone. She is a vegetarian who cries easily and cannot explain what she wants, and everyone keeps telling her to loosen up. Rohmer shot it on 16mm with a tiny crew and let Marie Rivière improvise, so the conversations have the cadence of real ones. The title refers to Jules Verne's novel about a flash of green at sunset that lets you read your own heart, which she overhears strangers discussing. The last scene is her waiting for it.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1986 and Cahiers' film of the year; the loosest and most affecting of Rohmer's Comedies and Proverbs, and the proof that a film made of a lonely woman's small talk could end in one of the great moments of grace in cinema.

title: Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives

editorial.hook: A dying farmer is visited by his dead wife and a son who became a monkey ghost.
editorial.synopsis: A farmer with kidney failure spends his last days on his tamarind farm in the northeast of Thailand, tended by his sister-in-law and a Laotian nurse. At dinner one evening the ghost of his dead wife fades in at the table, and then his long-lost son arrives from the forest — now a monkey spirit, black-furred, with glowing red eyes — and everyone is politely glad to see them. There is a princess and a talking catfish in a waterfall. There is a cave where the man thinks he was born. Apichatpong tells all of this at the speed of a warm evening, with no fear and no irony, and the effect is of being allowed into a world where death is not the end of the conversation.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 2010 — the first for a Thai film and the jury's choice under Tim Burton — and Cahiers' film of the year; the moment slow, spiritual, regional cinema took the world's biggest prize, and the clearest invitation into a way of seeing that has no Western equivalent.

editorial.hook: A British officer in the desert becomes something he can't control, in 70mm.
editorial.synopsis: A young British intelligence officer in Cairo during the First World War is sent to assess the Arab revolt against the Turks, and instead joins it, leads it, and begins to believe his own legend. Lean shot it over two years in Jordan, Morocco and Spain in 70mm, and the desert in it has never been equalled: a figure appearing as a shimmer on the horizon and taking two full minutes to arrive, a match cut from a flame to a sunrise, Maurice Jarre's theme swelling over dunes. But it is a character study at heart — Peter O'Toole, in his first major role, as a man who discovers he enjoys killing and cannot forgive himself, played with a strangeness that no epic hero had been allowed before.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 48 on TSPDT's list and the film that every director from Spielberg to Scorsese names as the reason they wanted to make films; the last great spectacle to be also a serious portrait of a self coming apart, and the standard for what a wide screen is for.

editorial.hook: An ad man mistaken for a spy who doesn't exist, from Manhattan to Mount Rushmore.
editorial.synopsis: A Madison Avenue advertising executive is mistaken in a hotel bar for a government agent who does not exist, kidnapped, poured full of bourbon and set loose on a cliff road. The rest of the film is him running — across the United Nations lobby, a train to Chicago with a blonde who may or may not be helping, a cornfield where a plane comes for him, an auction, a house above Mount Rushmore. Hitchcock called it the American Hitchcock film, and it is the lightest and most perfectly made of his thrillers: Cary Grant in a grey suit that never wrinkles, Bernard Herrmann's fandango, a wit so dry it can carry a plot that makes no sense at all. The crop-duster sequence has no music for seven minutes and is the model for every chase since.
editorial.whyItMatters: Forty-fifth in the 2022 critics' poll and the summit of Hitchcock's entertainments; the film that the Bond series was built to imitate, and the clearest example of his argument that style and suspense are the same thing.

editorial.hook: Five years hunting the Comanche who took his niece — and he may kill her when found.
editorial.synopsis: A man rides home to his brother's Texas ranch three years after the Civil War ended, from somewhere he will not name. Days later a Comanche raid kills the family and takes the two girls, and he sets out after them with a young man the family had adopted, who is one-eighth Cherokee and whom he can barely stand. The search lasts years. Ford shoots Monument Valley as he always did — the land as a cathedral — but this time the man in it, John Wayne, is a racist whose hatred is the engine of the film and whose heroism is never quite separable from it. The doorway shot that opens and closes the film has been quoted more than any other in American cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Fifteenth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and ninth on TSPDT's; the Western that turned the genre against itself, and the film that Scorsese, Schrader and Spielberg have each named as the one that taught them what a hero could hide — Taxi Driver is a remake of it.

editorial.hook: Her parents turn into pigs, and she must work in a bathhouse for spirits to get them back.
editorial.synopsis: A sullen girl is being driven to a new town by her parents when they take a wrong turn into a tunnel and find an abandoned theme park with a stall of steaming food. They eat; they become pigs; night falls and the park fills with spirits. To survive she must work in a vast bathhouse for the gods run by a witch, give up her name, and scrub a river spirit so polluted it arrives as a stink monster. Miyazaki draws a world with the density of a dream — soot sprites that carry coal, a masked spirit who eats staff, a train that runs across a flooded plain — and lets a child's fear and stubbornness be the whole plot. The train across a flooded plain near the end is the quietest sequence in animation.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 2002 — the first animated film to win — and 75th in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll; the film that took Japanese animation to the centre of world cinema and the clearest proof that a children's film can carry a culture's entire mythology.

editorial.hook: A woman falls asleep, and the same afternoon loops back with a knife and a key.
editorial.synopsis: A woman walks up a path to a house in the Hollywood hills, sees a figure in black with a mirror for a face turning the corner ahead, drops a key, picks up a flower, goes inside, and falls asleep in a chair. Then it happens again. And again, each time slightly wrong — the knife is in a different place, the key becomes the knife, there are three of her at the table drawing lots. Deren and her husband Alexander Hammid made it in their own house for a few hundred dollars, and in fourteen minutes they invented a language for the dream on film: the repeated action that changes, the stair that becomes a mountainside, the step from one place to another that lands somewhere else.
editorial.whyItMatters: Sixteenth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll — the highest-ranked short film and the highest-ranked work of the American avant-garde; Deren became the movement's founder and theorist, and every filmed dream since, from Lynch to Aronofsky, has her grammar in it.

editorial.hook: A French actress and a Japanese architect, one night in Hiroshima, and a memory of Nevers.
editorial.synopsis: A French actress in Hiroshima to make a film about peace spends a night and a day with a Japanese architect, and the film opens on their bodies, covered in what might be ash or sweat, while she tells him what she saw in the museum and he tells her she saw nothing. The city's horror is in the newsreels she describes; her own is in Nevers, during the war, a German soldier, a cellar, a shaved head — and the film cuts between the Japanese man's hand on a bed and the dead German's hand on a quay as if memory and the present were the same room. Marguerite Duras wrote it. Resnais made the first film in which editing is a form of thought, and the lovers' last exchange gives each other the names of their cities.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' second-best film of 1959 and the film that opened the French New Wave's other door — not Godard's jump cuts but Resnais' memory structures; the ancestor of every film that treats time as a wound rather than a line, from Marienbad to Mulholland Drive.

editorial.hook: An Armenian poet's life in tableaux: books drying on a roof, dyed wool, a conch shell.
editorial.synopsis: The life of Sayat-Nova, the eighteenth-century Armenian troubadour, told without narrative in a sequence of living pictures: books laid open on a monastery roof to dry in the wind, their pages turning; a boy with a conch to his ear; wool being dyed in vats; a woman and a man played by the same actress; lace, pomegranates bleeding onto cloth, a cherub stepping into a frame. Parajanov composes each shot flat and frontal like an icon or a Persian miniature and holds it until it becomes strange. There is no story to follow and the film says so at the start. Soviet censors found it incomprehensible and dangerous, recut it, and sent Parajanov to a labour camp a few years later.
editorial.whyItMatters: Ninety-third in the 2022 directors' poll and the most singular film in Soviet cinema; Parajanov invented a visual language out of Caucasian folk art and Orthodox iconography that has no predecessor and whose influence shows up in Tarsem, Lady Gaga videos and the whole idea of the film as tableau.

editorial.hook: A slaughterhouse worker in Watts, his family, and the weeks going by.
editorial.synopsis: A man who works in a Los Angeles slaughterhouse comes home tired and lies awake. His wife wants him to want her; his children play in the dirt lots and on the rooftops of Watts; friends come by with a stolen television, a plan to buy a car engine that falls off the back of a truck. Nothing much happens and everything does. Burnett shot it for under ten thousand dollars as his UCLA thesis, in black and white on weekends, with non-actors from the neighbourhood, and scored it to Dinah Washington, Paul Robeson and Earth, Wind & Fire — which is why music rights kept it out of release for thirty years. A couple slow-dancing to 'This Bitter Earth' in a bare living room is one of the great scenes in American film.
editorial.whyItMatters: Forty-third in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the founding work of the L.A. Rebellion; one of the first fifty films chosen for the National Film Registry, barely seen until its 2007 restoration, and the proof that American Neorealism existed — it was just not allowed to be shown.

editorial.hook: A photographer with a broken leg watches his neighbours, and one of them notices.
editorial.synopsis: A news photographer laid up with a broken leg in a Greenwich Village apartment during a heatwave spends his days watching the courtyard: a dancer, a composer, a lonely woman who sets a table for two, newlyweds behind a blind, and a salesman whose invalid wife is suddenly not there anymore. His girlfriend, too perfect for him in Edith Head gowns, thinks he's being morbid until she starts watching too. Hitchcock built the entire courtyard on one soundstage and never leaves the apartment; everything is seen through the window, through a lens, at a distance — until the distance collapses. It is a film about watching that implicates everyone watching it.
editorial.whyItMatters: Thirty-eighth in the 2022 critics' poll and Cahiers' top ten in 1955 — the New Wave critics' key text for Hitchcock as a moralist; the purest demonstration in cinema of point of view as structure, and the source of a hundred films about the ethics of looking.

editorial.hook: Dinner guests find, for no reason at all, that they cannot leave the room.
editorial.synopsis: A society dinner in a Mexico City mansion after the opera. The servants, one by one, make excuses and leave. The guests retire to the music room, and when it is time to go home, nobody goes — not because anything is stopping them, but because nobody can quite make themselves cross the threshold. Days pass. Water runs out. They break a pipe in the wall, eat the paper from the walls, turn on each other; a bear and a flock of sheep wander the house; a hand crawls across the floor. Buñuel offers no explanation and the film is the funnier and crueller for it. Outside, the police and a crowd gather at the gate and find they cannot go in.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' third-best film of 1963 and Buñuel's most perfect joke on the bourgeoisie; a parable about a class that cannot leave its own room, told with a straight face, and the direct ancestor of every film — from Dogtooth to Triangle of Sadness — that traps the rich with themselves.

editorial.hook: Two families in the humid north of Argentina, a filthy pool, and the heat at work.
editorial.synopsis: A hot, wet summer in the hills of northwest Argentina. A middle-aged woman falls drunk beside a swimming pool full of green water and cuts herself on the broken glasses, and nobody quite helps her. Her cousin brings her own children over. The teenagers lie on beds in the heat; the adults drink and complain about the Indian servants; someone is always on the point of going to Bolivia to buy school supplies and never does; a boy has a scar from a dog, or a rat, or a story about a rat. Martel's first film has no plot in the usual sense, only pressure: thunder that never quite breaks, a television showing a Virgin on a water tank, children with rifles in the forest, and a sense throughout that something terrible is a few feet off-screen.
editorial.whyItMatters: Winner of the Alfred Bauer Prize at Berlin in 2001 and the founding film of the New Argentine Cinema; Martel's sound design and sideways framing made her the most distinctive new voice in Latin American film, and this debut sits at 136 in the 2022 Sight & Sound poll.

editorial.hook: A Broadway star, a fan who wants her life, and the most quotable script ever written.
editorial.synopsis: A Broadway star at the top of her powers and the start of her forties is approached at the stage door by a young woman who has seen every performance and tells a sad story. The star takes her in as an assistant, and the assistant begins, with perfect modesty, to take everything. Mankiewicz tells it in flashback from an awards dinner with multiple narrators, and the dialogue — Bette Davis's 'Fasten your seatbelts', the critic Addison DeWitt's venom — is the most quoted in Hollywood for a reason: every line is a knife with a joke on the handle. It is about ambition, ageing and theatre, and it is also the most honest film Hollywood ever made about how women are used up by the business and by each other.
editorial.whyItMatters: Fourteen Academy Award nominations — a record it held alone for forty-seven years — and Cahiers' top ten in 1951; the film that made the case for the screenwriter as auteur, and whose structure of narrators and masks has been borrowed by every film about performance since.

editorial.hook: A bureaucrat learns he has months to live and tries, for once, to do one thing.
editorial.synopsis: A section chief in Tokyo's city hall has stamped papers for thirty years without being alive, and a doctor's evasions tell him he has stomach cancer and less than a year. He tries pleasure with a novelist in the bars; he tries youth with a young woman from the office who makes toy rabbits; neither works. Then a petition from some mothers about a sewage pit that should be a playground, which his department has been passing around for months, gives him something to do. Kurosawa cuts the film in half: the second part is his wake, where colleagues drink and argue about what he did and why. Takashi Shimura's face, singing a song in a swing in the snow, is the image the film is remembered by.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 106 on TSPDT's list and the Kurosawa film people who dislike Kurosawa love; a study of a modest life redeemed, built on an audacious structure — the hero dies at the midpoint — that proved the director's humanism could be as formally bold as his epics.

editorial.hook: A noble family scattered into slavery in medieval Japan, watched from a distance.
editorial.synopsis: Eleventh-century Japan. A provincial governor is exiled for defending his peasants, and his wife and two small children set out to join him. On the way they are tricked by a priestess, separated by slavers: the mother sold to a brothel on an island, the children to the estate of Sansho, a bailiff who brands runaways on the forehead. Ten years pass. The boy grows hard; the girl keeps the father's words alive — 'without mercy, man is like a beast.' Mizoguchi films it in long, flowing takes that stay at a distance even from the worst of it, as if looking directly would be indecent, and the film's cruelty and tenderness are inseparable. The last scene on a beach is the most merciful ending in cinema and the most devastating.
editorial.whyItMatters: Silver Lion at Venice in 1954 and 75th in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll; Mizoguchi's long take — the camera as a witness that refuses to cut away — is the root of a tradition that runs through Hou Hsiao-hsien and Angelopoulos, and this is its highest expression.

editorial.hook: A trench-coated agent in a city ruled by a computer that outlawed love — shot in Paris.
editorial.synopsis: A secret agent drives into Alphaville, a city on another planet ruled by a computer that has abolished emotion and poetry — executions are held in a swimming pool with synchronised swimmers — to find a missing agent and destroy the machine. Godard shot it in Paris without a single set: the Electricité de France building, hotel corridors, highways at night, neon signs, all made alien by the camera. Eddie Constantine, a B-movie tough guy, plays the agent with a face like a cliff; Anna Karina plays the computer's daughter, who has never heard the word 'love' and learns it from a book of Éluard poems he carries. It is a science-fiction film with no special effects, which is the joke and also the point.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 1965 and the film that proved the future is just the present seen correctly; its method — genre as a frame for philosophy, the modern city as dystopia without alteration — fed directly into Blade Runner, Brazil and every science fiction that found the future in the architecture already around it.

title: Once Upon a Time in the West

editorial.hook: Three men wait ten minutes for a train, and the Western is never the same.
editorial.synopsis: Three gunmen wait at a railway halt in the desert for a train, and Leone makes you wait with them for ten minutes: a fly on a face, water dripping onto a hat, a windmill creaking. Then the train comes, and a man with a harmonica gets off. The plot — a widow, a railroad baron, a hired killer with a child's blue eyes, land that is worth something because the rails are coming — is mythic and simple; the film is about faces in extreme close-up, horizons in widescreen, and Ennio Morricone's score, written before shooting so the actors could move to it. Henry Fonda, cast against a lifetime of decency, plays the villain. It is an elegy for a genre made by someone who loved it from the outside.
editorial.whyItMatters: Forty-sixth in the 2022 directors' poll and the summit of the Italian Western; Leone's operatic time — stretching waiting into ceremony — is the direct ancestor of Tarantino, of slow cinema's long takes, and of the idea that a genre picture can be a requiem.

editorial.hook: A mutiny over rotten meat, a massacre on a staircase, and the cut as a weapon.
editorial.synopsis: Sailors on a Russian battleship in 1905 refuse to eat soup made from maggot-ridden meat, and an officer orders them shot. The crew mutinies. The ship sails into Odessa, where the city turns out in sympathy, and on the great staircase down to the harbour Cossack troops advance on the crowd in ranks. Eisenstein cut that sequence from dozens of shots — a mother carrying her dead son up the steps against the flow, a pram bouncing down them, a woman's shattered glasses — into six minutes that compress and stretch time until the event becomes a feeling rather than a record. The film was commissioned as propaganda for the twentieth anniversary of the revolution. It became a theory of cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 20 on TSPDT's list and the most influential film ever made about editing; the Odessa Steps sequence has been quoted by everyone from Brian De Palma to Terry Gilliam, and Eisenstein's idea that meaning is made between shots rather than inside them is the foundation of film grammar.

editorial.hook: Four desperate men drive two trucks of nitroglycerine over three hundred miles.
editorial.synopsis: A squalid town somewhere in Latin America, full of Europeans with no money and no way out. An American oil company has a fire at a well three hundred miles away and needs nitroglycerine to put it out, and the only way to get it there is by truck over mountain roads, with no suspension, no shock absorbers, and a bonus for anyone who survives. Four men take the job. Clouzot spends an hour letting you learn the town's heat and boredom and contempt, so that when the trucks start moving every pothole is a detonation. A hairpin turn on a rotting wooden platform; a boulder in the road; a lake of oil. It is the most sustained suspense sequence in cinema and it is also a film about how men treat each other when fear strips them.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or and Golden Bear in 1953 — the only film to win both — and the model for the existential thriller: Friedkin remade it as Sorcerer, and its first hour of atmosphere before any action is the lesson that tension is built, not staged.
